title: The long history of hunting
gist: Caroline Eden reviews Brian Fagan's posthumous 'Hunting: The Pursuit That Shaped Humanity', drawing out its most useful non-obvious thread: hunting functioned as governance infrastructure for the British Raj - shikar parties were intelligence-gathering and grievance-management events - while conservation emerged from within the hunting class itself, through figures like Roosevelt and George Bird Grinnell. Fagan is blunt that trophy hunters' conservation claims are nonsense.

themes.theme: Hunting as a tool of governance

insights.claim: The British Raj embraced local Indian hunting as a means of gaining control over unfamiliar places, with shikar parties serving as venues for addressing political grievances and gathering intelligence.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Informal, social settings as the actual machinery of colonial administration - a reusable lens for how influence is exercised where formal institutions are thin.
insights.quote: Shikar (Bengali for hunting) parties were useful events for addressing political grievances and gaining intelligence.
insights.locator: The British Raj, keen to advance its commercial

insights.claim: British officials spent much of their time testing the loyalty of local rulers and expanding into hostile areas, using hunts for 'endless opportunities for low-key conversations that quietly smoothed over controversies'.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Relationship maintenance, not force, did the day-to-day work of imperial control - the cheapest available instrument of governance.
insights.quote: eating and sleeping among them and having endless opportunities for low-key conversations that quietly smoothed over controversies
insights.locator: It was also an opportunity for the British to mingle

insights.claim: Over the centuries in India hunting parties were organised so that nobles and rulers could showcase power and privilege, and only later became an integral part of governance - status display preceding administrative function.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Practices adopted for prestige can acquire hard institutional functions later; watch for the same drift in today's elite rituals.

insights.claim: Lord Curzon inaugurated the Keoladeo reserve in 1902 with an organised duck shoot in which his party shot a few hundred birds, while Lord Linlithgow set the record in 1938 by downing 4,273 birds in a single day.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: A precise baseline for how recently extraction at this scale was normal in what is now a protected sanctuary - Keoladeo only became a National Park in 1981.
insights.quote: the record was held by Lord Linlithgow, another viceroy of India, who in 1938 downed 4,273 birds in a single day
insights.locator: When Lord Curzon, Viceroy of India

insights.claim: The late 19th-century fashion for aigrettes turned wild bird feathers into a multimillion-dollar trade that killed about five million birds annually across roughly 50 US species, with hunters destroying entire rookeries and leaving carcasses to decay.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: A documented case of a consumer fashion cycle driving industrial-scale ecological destruction - and of how fast it collapsed when fashion changed.
insights.quote: This millinery resulted in the slaughter of about five million birds annually, everything from ducks and egrets to larks – about 50 US species

insights.claim: The plume trade was ended not by regulation alone but by the anti-plume movement combined with the First World War bringing more sombre fashions - demand-side collapse, not supply-side enforcement.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Exogenous shifts in consumer taste can extinguish a destructive industry faster than policy; a precedent for how extractive consumer markets actually die.
insights.quote: Things shifted with the arrival of the anti-plume movement, and the outbreak of the First World War, which brought with it more sombre fashions.

insights.claim: Birds were eventually valued as agents of insect pest control benefiting human health and agriculture, notably after major grasshopper outbreaks on the Plains - the economic case arriving after the moral one.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Ecosystem services are typically priced only after the resource is depleted and the cost becomes visible in output.

themes.theme: Conservation came from inside the hunting class

insights.claim: Theodore Roosevelt was photographed dressed as a deer hunter in 1885 and was simultaneously a leading force in founding US conservation societies - hunters and conservationists converge rather than simply oppose each other.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: The constituency that consumes a resource can be the one that protects it, which matters for how environmental coalitions are actually built.

insights.claim: George Bird Grinnell, who edited Forest and Stream from 1880 to 1911, ran a successful campaign to outlaw the use of dogs and lights for hunting deer and was deeply involved in preventing a railroad through Yellowstone - journalism functioning as conservation infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Media ownership as a durable lever on regulatory outcomes; Grinnell's 30-year editorship is what made the campaigns work.
insights.quote: Grinnell edited an influential magazine, Forest and Stream, from 1880 to 1911, and among his achievements was that he headed a successful campaign to outlaw the use of dogs and lights for hunting deer.
insights.locator: more attention is given to a wildlife conservationist

insights.claim: Grinnell witnessed the last great Pawnee buffalo hunt in 1856, when 1,000 horsemen killed 1,000 buffalo in a day by encircling them as they scattered to ease butchering.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Indigenous hunting also operated at industrial scale, complicating any simple pre-colonial equilibrium narrative.
insights.quote: when 1,000 horsemen killed 1,000 buffalo in a day, encircling them as they scattered for ease of butchering – the women’s task

insights.claim: Fagan dismisses trophy-hunting organisations' conservation claims outright as nonsense, on the grounds that they are hunting animals in captivity or with restricted movement.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the sustainable-use justification that underpins the legal trophy-hunting industry's licence to operate.
insights.quote: Many trophy-hunting organisations claim that they are engaged in long-term conservation of game stocks. This is, of course, nonsense. They are hunting animals in captivity, or with restricted movement.

insights.claim: Archaic hunting required far closer contact with prey than rifle shooting - Neanderthal weapons were lethal but their effectiveness depended on stalking and close-quarters killing, and humans also scavenged carcasses other predators had already killed.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Technology, not intent, changed the ecological footprint of hunting - the constraint was always range and risk.
insights.quote: Neanderthal hunting weapons were ‘sharp and lethal, but their effectiveness depended on stalking’ and close-quarters killing.
insights.locator: Archaic human hunts required far closer contact

insights.claim: Fagan argues that once domestication gave humans the opportunity to live alongside animals with care, the relationship instead became 'often crueler and more exploitative' - proximity increased rather than reduced cruelty.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Counters the assumption that closer human-animal integration improves welfare, with implications for how modern livestock systems are assessed.
insights.quote: Instead, Fagan writes, the relationship became ‘often crueler and more exploitative.’
insights.locator: Later, when domesticated animals assumed a more central role

insights.claim: Women are treated as drivers rather than passive participants in hunting history - Xenophon, who kept a hunting ground near Sparta in the fourth century BC, held that women who hunted had the blessing of the goddess Artemis.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: A corrective to the default framing of hunting as exclusively male, supported by classical evidence.
